Dragan Djokanovic: If there was any discipline, there should have been better responses to, to these, these provocations. Radovan Karadzic: Yes, yes. That's right, that's right. Dragan Djokanovic: But tell me, were there any discussions with the SDA last night? Radovan Karadzic: Yes, there were. Dragan Djokanovic: So how is it going? Radovan Karadzic: Well, it's going fine. I think it's going fine. Dragan Djokanovic: All right. Radovan Karadzic: I think it's going fine. If we stick to what we have said and so, I mean without ... Dragan Djokanovic: Without any ... Our side is holding on it ... Radovan Karadzic: Yes, we'll see. Dragan Djokanovic: Nikola told me yesterday that you gave him the paper they asked for. Radovan Karadzic: Yes, yes, that's right. Dragan Djokanovic: So now I need to get a written answer too. Radovan Karadzic: Yes, they've ... Well maybe some experts should be appointed to do that or something. Dragan Djokanovic: But tell me the, that, what the other night was ... Yutel, these papers that are circling, have they done any damage? Radovan Karadzic: I don't believe they have done any damage, I think they have just contributed to, to hating Serbs more but that is ... But those who want to hate, they hate anyways and those, those who do not want to hate, they don't even believe in that. That is, those are forgeries. That is ... Dragan Djokanovic: Oh yeah. And are you okay otherwise? Radovan Karadzic: I'm fine, thank God. Dragan Djokanovic: Are you an optimist for -- regardless of all of this that is. Radovan Karadzic: Well, I think I am, I think I am. I think it is going, that things will start taking some natural course or something. Dragan Djokanovic: Right. Okay, Doctor. It was nice hearing from you. Radovan Karadzic: Thank you. Till soon. Dragan Djokanovic: Thank you very much. Radovan Karadzic: Have a nice day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm informed that the -- that a better way to proceed with these intercepts would be to provide individual CDs and so with the leave of Your Honour, that's the way we will proceed with these intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as long as your case manager and the registrar agree on the matter, we're only too glad to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, do you recognise the voices on that telephone intercept?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: This was a conversation between Dr. Karadzic and myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time, Dr. Djokanovic, were you following closely the events in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall whether I was following closely but I was following, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After discussions of the events in Croatia, you and Dr. Karadzic discuss a topic which is not entirely clear from the text of this intercept. Do you recall specifically what discussions you were referring to at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: At this point in time, I don't think if it was the supporters of the Croatian policy or some individual parties, but they were launching attacks against the JNA barracks, blocking any food supplies from being delivered to them. I'm telling you what I knew from the mass media. And we were all quite wondering at the JNA's behaviour that was quite soft, so to say, they did not really protect their men or property, so that I welcomed the press release issued by the JNA command in Belgrade that we were going to protect and defend the JNA barracks. This was a press release that was politically favorable for us in Bosnia and Herzegovina because the public in Bosnia and Herzegovina had to understand that the JNA was going to do its best to preserve the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that it was not going to allow it to be dismantled that easily. I sent a letter to Mr. Karadzic, I'm trying to remember now what it was all about, because at that point, we were preparing the plebescite for the Serbian people. I believe it was an invitation for a multiparty meeting to be held at Holiday Inn in Sarajevo just before the holding of the Serbian plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, on the table before you is a text from Oslobodjenje. In the course of one of your answers from the president's questions, you mentioned a text that was published, is this the text that you were referring to? I'm referring to Exhibit P543.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: It is possible that this is the text. It is quite possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, could you just take a moment to read that text and then I'll take you to specific parts of it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the text -- just to confirm, is that the text that you wrote and was published in Oslobodjenje in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the text that I wrote and which was published in the Sarajevo Oslobodjenje on the 3rd of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this text, you write that the war that could break out could be the most disastrous and catastrophic war, interethnic and interreligious. In fact you say that "the BH could be engulfed by the most catastrophic ethnic and religious war of the kind unknown in history to date." Further on, you say that"Yugoslavia exists as a federal state and that its constitution guarantees equality to the republics and the right to self-determination to the people living in on its territory. Just by proceeding from this fact, it is possible to coordinate the national interests of Muslims, Serbs and Croats and resolve the political crisis in BH in a peaceful and democratic way. If either one of these parties decides to ignore this fact it risks drawing its people into the madness of a fratricidal war." As at October 1991, was it your view that if the Muslims and Croats proceeded with their aim to establish an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina the results you have detailed in this transcript may occur?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I believed at the time and I wrote at the time. But unfortunately, the events that followed showed us what actually -- what course the events took. Nobody was prepared to strike a compromise. They did not play with their cards on the table. They did not take into account the future interests and a war broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your view, were the Muslims informed of the position of the Serbs openly and clearly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They were certainly aware because it was all done openly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it clear to you at this time which group in this potential conflict had the support from Serbia and from the federal institutions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: This isn't a difficult question. The Croatian people enjoyed the support of Croatia. The Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina enjoyed the support of the Serbs from Serbia, whereas the Bosnian Muslims could only rely upon what they themselves did in Bosnia and Herzegovina and on their self-organising they probably had the inclination of some of the countries abroad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In light of that position, at this time when you produced this text, what did you expect the Muslim response to be to this position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I would very much like to hear the answer also to the second part of your question, that's of course what are the consequences? In your earlier question, you refer to support of the Serbs and of the federal institutions. The witness answered that -- did not give an answer in respect of the federal institutions. Could you please invite him to do so?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, His Honour has observed that the question related to both Serbia and the federal institutions. In your answer, you've referred to support from Croatia, support from Serbia. Could you tell the Court who you thought would receive support from the federal institutions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: In this text, I did not tackle these issues. I only stated that at that point in time, Yugoslavia existed as a state under the international law, that all of its federal institutions were valid because if it was a state under the international law, then all its institutions were fully valid because the official policy of both Serbia and Montenegro was to stay in Yugoslavia. The Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina were never insecure about remaining within Yugoslavia which meant that the other two sides, Serbs -- Croats and Muslims had to count with such a position. The Serbs therefore had the friendly support of Montenegro and Serbia, they could count on the official governments of Montenegro and Serbia as well as of the federal institutions that were in existence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In light of the support of the states being behind either the Croats or the Serbs, what did you anticipate the Muslims would seek in their negotiations with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: What was quite unclear to me and to many at the time was the position of the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina because they did not speak their minds openly about the policies of Croatia and they did support the SDA political agenda for an independent BiH. With this text, I wanted to launch a discussion among the Croat intellectuals in Bosnia and Herzegovina on this issue because if Croatia was seceding from Yugoslavia and Croats were also a sovereign and constituent nation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, what was their position on this? Did they support the secession of Croatia? Did they want to remain within Bosnia and Herzegovina? Did they want BiH to remain within Yugoslavia? Or what else was on their mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will ask you to slow down. Please proceed. Was that the end of your answer? Of course, that didn't make much sense to ask you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only had a couple more things to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. If you just look at the text, when it stops moving, you continue. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had we known the views of Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it would have been much more easier to reconcile the views of the other two peoples because this was the main bone of contention in the earlier talks taking place in summer, like the discussion with Zulfikarpasic, then an Belgrade initiative launched by the Belgrade politicians supported by Mr. Krajisnik, president of the Assembly which was at -- in any case a very positive initiative. That would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred to support that the Serbs may gain from federal institutions. Which federal institutions were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't thinking about the support at the time the way you're thinking now with hindsight, I was talking about the federal state, the federal constitution that formed part of international law and could not easily be dismantled. And if we choose to remain within Yugoslavia, then that's the side we are on. I did not really think of a specific federal organ that we could draw upon. But in any way, one knows which federal institutions one can draw upon if one is faced with a specific problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time in October 1991, was it clear to you what could happen to the Muslims and their interests if they proceeded to declare an independent state of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: They were unable to proclaim an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina on their own. They had to have a parliamentary majority comprising deputies from the Muslim political parties and some other deputies either from Serb or Croat parties. At that point, it was useless to expect the Serbs to support them in the parliament but one could expect the support of the HDZ. There was this constant threat of this unprincipled parliamentary majority forming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the Muslims able to protect themselves if war broke out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: At that point, I was only envisaging the possibility of this catastrophe taking place, but I was not going into any details in that relation. I just knew that we could be faced with catastrophe that we had already seen recorded in history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I would normally not give any comment to a question to you, especially not if the Defence had not raised any objection. But it is implicit in your question: Were the Muslims able to protect themselves in war broke out? That there was one party which had to protect which suggests a lot which I think should not be implicit in the question, especially not in chief. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will rephrase that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In light of the relative strength of the state institutions behind the Croats, the Serbs, and the Muslims, what was the relative position in terms of armaments of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, no foundation has been laid for a question of that nature in terms of the witness's knowledge of the position in terms of the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness, I think the witness's testimony on his position would give a presumption of any knowledge. But if he doesn't have any of it, then he'll certainly tell us. Could you please answer the question put to you by Mr. Margetts, that is: In light of the relative strength of the state institutions behind the Croats, the Serbs, and the Muslims, what was the relative position in terms of armaments of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the media, specifically from the interview with Mr. Zulfikarpasic, we looked at it earlier on, I had occasion to see that the Party of Democratic Action was getting armed. What sort of armaments could those have been in relation to those held by Croatia or by the federal state that had enormous military resources. Whatever they were able to purchase and obtain was nothing in relation to what in future Croatia and Serbia and Montenegro could have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, I understand that you attended the session of the SRBiH assembly held on 15 October 1991, when the SDA placed the memorandum of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the agenda. Could you relate to the Court what your experience was on the evening of the 14th of October, 1991 and during the course of that session on 15 October 1991.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, this was the crucial ground breaking moment in Bosnia-Herzegovina because for the earlier -- for the nine months preceding this session, this declaration for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina was hanging above our heads. But we need an introduction before answering this question, which is: Why did Mr. Krajisnik become the president of the BiH Assembly. Perhaps not even Mr. Krajisnik himself knows this. Prior to the election in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Karadzic and I talked about the division of function in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Dr. Karadzic told me that Izetbegovic had offered him to pick out a function that the Serbs wanted, whether they wanted to have the function of the president of the Presidency of BiH or whether they wanted the function of the president of the assembly, which was second in power, or the third in power which was the prime minister's function which belonged to the third nation in BiH, that is the Croats. I was in favour of the Serb being the president of the Presidency because in this capacity, he represents the BiH and he is the final instance in the adoption of laws, whereas Karadzic thought that whatever was to be passed at the expense of the Serbs was going to be passed in the parliament and that therefore it was much better for the Serbs to have the position of the president of the assembly. Now, the choice had to be made which Serb was to be chosen. I know that I was nominated by the constituency in Foca. There, they wanted Vojo Maksimovic who hailed from Foca to be president of the parliament; however, I told -- and I offered this to Karadzic but he turned this down. They said that they had Velibor Ostojic who was an official of the SDS who was to be preferred for this position. He told me in this talk, "Yes, I accepted this argumentation of his that the man of ours in the parliament could help prevent the passage of such an anti-constitutional and constitutional document." So talking about Karadzic -- with Karadzic about Mr. Krajisnik as a possible speaker of the assembly he knew that he knew him from before, that they were similar in temperament and character. In fact their parents were alike. Of course, I didn't know Mr. Krajisnik except by sight at that time. I had only seen him at a panel discussion before the elections in Bosnia. This was in Novo Sarajevo at a meeting in the Vaso Pelagic culture centre and he was there on the working Presidency, the chair that had prepared this panel discussion. So Mr. Krajisnik was given the role of protecting the interests of the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina through his position of president of parliament and, indeed, throughout that period until that very night, he kept warning at different meetings and publicly as well of the fact that the declaration that was in the offing by the deputies of the SDS and was being advocated by them as well as by the politicians, and it was being referred to by politicians in the media that it was the danger and that there was something which was cause for concern. On the eve of this assembly, a Serbian friend of mine called me and he told me that the top leadership of the Party of Democratic Action had decided for the document to be adopted in the Assembly. In fact he told me that the then minister of foreign affairs of Germany had directly talked to Izetbegovic and had told him, "You just bring that paper to the Hague." And the plan was made to the effect that the Assembly can last up to 12 hours or rather to mid-day. This was the day when he travelled from the Butmir airport in Sarajevo to The Hague. That evening, I informed Dr. Karadzic of this. I called him by telephone late at night and he told me, "We'll see each other in the morning in my -- in Mr. Krajisnik's," rather, "office." Early that morning, we did meet at Mr. Krajisnik's office and I told them this. They were quite silent and without any comment. I gained the impression that seeing that I had learned this from my own sources, that they, too, seeing the influence that they wielded which was greater than mine, had also learned of this and it was no surprise. However, during that day as the time passed and the time passed also in terms of what could realistically be done in my view, and my view was that we had to make this information public, that we had to make this known to both the Bosnia and the Yugoslav and the world public, namely what was being prepared in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was, in fact, in favour of inviting the people to take to the streets and demonstrate, seeing what was in for them. But time was running out and I said -- in fact, Mr. Krajisnik told me that morning, "Doctor, I have a remedy. I have a drug for that." And I was quite relaxed that day. Then I finally asked what kind of remedy are you talking about? He told me the rules of procedure, according to the rules of procedure of the assembly, he was entitled to adjourn in the session of the assembly and that according to that same rule of the procedure of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, no one had the right to reconvene the Assembly and have it continue its work.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: So I was consternated. I said look, they are not even observing the constitution, why would they abide by the rules of procedure. However, that's the way it was and that's the way it remained. Mr. Krajisnik adjourned the Assembly session. We went to his office, Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and I, that is, and then we watched the continuation of that Assembly session on television. The vice president of the Assembly, Mario Ljubic a Croatian deputy, actually unlawfully, opened the Assembly session. They adopted this memorandum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina against the will of the Serbian deputies. That was this defining moment, this turnabout which actually paved the way to war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, can you describe the position of speaker of the Bosnian parliament to the Court?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: In the orders as we have in the book, the speaker of the Assembly is the second in rank after the president of the state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of effective power in the Bosnian state, what type of power does the speaker of the Assembly have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I could not say. I could not speak of -- in terms of these categories or the extent of their respective powers because I'm not a lawyer to be able to gauge that precisely. But in any case, that was the position with quite a lot of political clout and access to the media as well and in the particular case of Mr. Krajisnik, he very adroitly used this position of speaker of parliament and he had this fantastic media promotion, he was accepted by the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In fact, at a certain point in time, Mr. Milosevic at one of these meetings of ours, I think it was in June, he said that Mr. Krajisnik was the best president of Assembly in the area of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the Muslims introduced the memorandum to the agenda, what did Mr. Krajisnik do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I have already described all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Dr. Djokanovic, I understand that there was a meeting in the morning at the office of Momcilo Krajisnik where you and Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik discussed the pending memorandum. I just want to be entirely clear as to what occurred during the course of the day and the sequence of events. So if you could bear with me and just tell me, possibly again, what Mr. Krajisnik did when the memorandum was introduced to the agenda?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: When this memorandum was placed on the agenda, the only possibility apart from what I was advocating, extra parliamentary demonstrations, warnings to the foreign and domestic media, et cetera of what might happen and would happen. The Serbian deputies did the only thing they could at that moment which was to take the floor one by one to keep warning of these things but this was calculated. This was reckoned with, in fact, in advance, because it was the time allotted to each deputy to take the floor which was something which was known. So the Muslims and the Serbs, the Muslim and the Bosnian -- excuse me, deputies did not take the floor at all and only waited for the vote so Mr. Krajisnik knew that this would happen. I cannot recall with precision what he said to them before the conclusion of the Assembly but I do remember that he concluded the Assembly session in a quite legalistic fashion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the Serbs took the floor, what did they say? What did they tell the Muslims and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I was so worried because I also knew some things that the deputies didn't know and I did not exactly follow their speeches. You can see that from the verbatim records of the proceedings. I cannot tell you what they spoke about at this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not Dr. Karadzic spoke?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: It is impossible that Dr. Karadzic did not speak at that Assembly and warned the deputies of these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that he did speak and, if so, do you recall what he said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what I'm going to say but I think that this was it. Karadzic's warning was the kind of warning that was often circulated in the media, namely, the sentence in the event of war between the Serbs and the Croats, there will be no longer any Muslims, but I'm not quite sure that this was so in that particular instance. I'm not quite sure that that was at that meeting, at that session, it was either at that or at some previous session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to move to the next exhibit which is an intercept of telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to ask one question. Witness, if I understood correctly, you have told us that Mr. Krajisnik had concluded the session and that after that, you went to his office. With whom did you go to his office? Who was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also, if I understood correctly, Mr. Krajisnik and yourself, you were able to follow over a television set what was going on in the Assembly? And what did you notice, what were you able to see? That the session continued? It was reconvened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a live TV transmission so that the public in Bosnia and Herzegovina could follow the session and of course we, who were there where the TV set was, followed it to the end and then we left the Assembly building, the three of us. Mr. Krajisnik offered me a ride to my place but I walked home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But my question was rather the following: What was the reaction of Mr. Krajisnik when he saw that the session was reconvened, that it was continuing? He had suspended the session, and in his absence, the session had continued; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were simply consternated, everything that we had done before, everything that we had tried to impress before the people before by way of a warning was actually happening. We knew that it would happen but we wanted it not to happen. But simply all of the time we were aware that there could bestruck this principle, the parliamentary majority coalition and that they would actually accept and adopt whatever they felt like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... able to react, to intern, because he was able to see what was going on? Could he have gone back to the Assembly? Could he have said something, done something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, at that point, there was no possibility for him to do anything at all. The mood in the Assembly was such, they actually jumped at the opportunity when I say they, I mean the Bosnian and the Croatian deputies. They were very happy when the Serbs left the Assembly so that they were quite euphoric and adopted this. They had decided to do that and that is why they did it as we would say, come what may or come hill or high water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the atmosphere in Mr. Krajisnik's office while you were watching this over the television? What were the comments? What was said between the three of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we were defeated. We abstained from any comments. We just wanted to get out of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to move to the next exhibit which is an intercepted telephone conversation. It's number 17 on the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This CD will be Prosecution Exhibit P544 and the transcript P544A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: This is the intercept dated 20 October, 1991. Your Honour, unfortunately we're having a technical problem with that intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see it. The two options are either you wait for it after the break or you work on the basis of the written document at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're content to proceed without playing this intercept. We'll proceed on the basis of the written document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, do you have before you a transcript of a telephone conversation between yourself and Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just for identification purposes, at the top of that transcript does it state CD-21-20-3/02/014?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll read this intercept into the record or if it could be read into the record by the interpreters? I'll proceed to read it in if Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you need every single part of it so it should be read in as a whole or you read the relevant parts because then we get all the good evenings and all can I speak to the doctors with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just wondering if it might be a better idea to take the break and see if this issue can be resolved so that we can deal with the intercept in the normal manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is a suggestion, I take it, Mr. Margetts, you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's acceptable to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Djokanovic, we hope to resolve the technical problems in respect of the next intercept during a break, a break which will last for 20 minutes. We'll resume at 20 minutes to 1.00 of this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see yellow highlighted on my screen Mr. Margetts, "a known person, good evening." That sounds promising.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it all looks very positive so referring to Prosecution Exhibit P544 if we could play that intercept.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Unidentified Speaker: Good evening. Radovan Karadzic: Good evening. Unidentified Speaker: Is that Karadzic residence. Radovan Karadzic: Yes, it is. Unidentified Speaker: Dragan Djokanovic wishes to speak to the doctor. Dragan Djokanovic: Hello. Radovan Karadzic: Yes. Dragan Djokanovic: Good evening. Radovan Karadzic: Good evening, how are you? Dragan Djokanovic: Very well, thank you. And yourself? Radovan Karadzic: The line is poor, just a moment. Dragan Djokanovic: Hello. Radovan Karadzic: Hello. Dragan Djokanovic: Is it any better now? Radovan Karadzic: It's better now. Dragan Djokanovic: So you've returned today? Radovan Karadzic: Yes, yes. Dragan Djokanovic: Any success over there? Radovan Karadzic: Yes, excellent. Dragan Djokanovic: Excellent, I was worried how it would turn out. Radovan Karadzic: It was good, good, excellent. Dragan Djokanovic: Good. Radovan Karadzic: You see, Mi ... Milad has wrong ideas, but we've dealt with it. Dragan Djokanovic: Yeah, goodness knows I was afraid of this hot temper of his. Radovan Karadzic: Yeah, but we've dealt with it. Dragan Djokanovic: Err ... Radovan Karadzic: He doesn't have more than two or three persons who support him, but we've managed to convince them as well. Dragan Djokanovic: Great. So in the course of the next week your ideas will have been implemented? Radovan Karadzic: Yes, yes. Everything runs its course. We won't start -- be the first to start with anything and whatever they offer us we have to accept, there's no other way. Dragan Djokanovic: Yes. Radovan Karadzic: And you are ... Are you okay? Dragan Djokanovic: Well, I am, I'm receiving somehow constantly in expectation so one doesn't really know if he feels good or bad. Radovan Karadzic: Don't worry, everything is going to be okay. Dragan Djokanovic: They have to give in now. He has found himself, particularly now after The Hague, he has found himself in a tight corner, I think. Radovan Karadzic: Who? Dragan Djokanovic: Alija. Radovan Karadzic: Well, ha ha ha, it's his fault. What did he think, that he can make political crime and play games with Serbs, he ... made a small trick. That's not the way. It's an embarrassment for him. I told him there at the negotiations and I also said it publicly that it was going to be embarrassing for him and it is embarrassing. Dragan Djokanovic: Yes, yes. Radovan Karadzic: But what's done, it's done, no way back, let them do whatever they think is good for their people, good for them. We'll help them fight for their people. But they cannot sacrifice our Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. people for their people. Dragan Djokanovic: Of course. Radovan Karadzic: Nor shall we ask for them to make sacrifices for us. Let -- we have news that Boras was up there in the Posavina region and that he brought -- a decision was brought to unite that region up there with Croatia. Dragan Djokanovic: Uh-huh. Radovan Karadzic: So, Croats are very busy with the regionalisation. We are -- we know about it they have made maps and rounded up the regions before we did. Dragan Djokanovic: Of course. Of course. I expect a conflict between SDA and HDZ one of these days. Radovan Karadzic: There will be a conflict because they want to take more. Dragan Djokanovic: Yes. Radovan Karadzic: Take Travnik, for example. Muslims make a relative majority there, and Croats want Travnik for themselves. Dragan Djokanovic: Yes. They say that Travnik is their territory ... Radovan Karadzic: Yes, based on the historical rights, because there was this Banovina Hrvatska and -- so let them have it. And our territories are quite ethnically clean and we'll easily agree with the Muslims. There are our people at their territory and these other guys, let them. Dragan Djokanovic: I think that it would be wise to go public with this idea that Serbs wish to compromise with Muslims. Radovan Karadzic: No way. People would replace me immediately, no way. They have spat on us. We have offered them brotherly love hundreds of times, have offered them a hand of friendship. Dragan Djokanovic: Yes, yes. Radovan Karadzic: Like ... Dragan Djokanovic: It's well known what they are like. Radovan Karadzic: You saw how they behave at the club, they don't allow me to even see Izetbegovic not so much as to talk to him. Dragan Djokanovic: Yes I saw it but I thought that because of the Muslims ... Radovan Karadzic: I don't want to for Muslim's sake, let the Muslims say no, let them say that they are against such policy and let Alija say yes we were wrong, we want to go together with Serbs. But he has to say it publicly. Dragan Djokanovic: Yes, poor him now, now, he knows he has to say it, but how is he going to say it. Radovan Karadzic: No way, no way. I would be politically dead if I offered him a hand now. Dragan Djokanovic: You are right. Radovan Karadzic: No way. There's not a single Serb that would ... Bulatovic would loose power in Montenegro. Dragan Djokanovic: Yes. Just look at what he has done over there. Radovan Karadzic: So I'm talking to my brother, I said we want to spare him in our declaration not to touch him. He said no, don't spare him. He and the government won't endure much longer. Dragan Djokanovic: Have you heard how Kibarda attacked him yesterday. Radovan Karadzic: No, I haven't heard anything. Dragan Djokanovic: He had a press conference in Herceg Novi. Radovan Karadzic: Yes. Dragan Djokanovic: And I said that it was a shame, horrible shame. Radovan Karadzic: Yes. Yes. Dragan Djokanovic: Who was forcing him. He could have, if he didn't know he could have restrained himself. Radovan Karadzic: Look, brother, and just to think that the Assembly authorised him, instructed him in fact, to act based on his own estimates. Dragan Djokanovic: And he ... Radovan Karadzic: So the betrayal is his, it has nothing to do with the Assembly. Dragan Djokanovic: That's right. Okay. So you go with your plan this week, right? Radovan Karadzic: Yes, yes. Everything runs its course. Dragan Djokanovic: Okay. Radovan Karadzic: Good. Dragan Djokanovic: It was good hearing from you. I'm glad that everything went well in Banja Luka. Radovan Karadzic: We invite you, on that day. Dragan Djokanovic: Thank you ... Radovan Karadzic: Okay. Dragan Djokanovic: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: This intercept P544 has the date 20 October 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, do you recognise the voices in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: That's a conversation between Dr. Karadzic and myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall having this conversation with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I refer you to the first page, there's an exchange between yourself and Dr. Karadzic and you ask Dr. Karadzic whether he had any success over there. Do you know where it is you're referring to and what it is you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The 20th of October, 1991, which means a couple of days after the adoption of the declaration by the Assembly, the document was sent to The Hague. I don't know if there was Mr. Milosevic or Mr. Karadzic who were in The Hague or maybe it was Mr. Karadzic going to meet with Mr. Milosevic in Belgrade, so they discussed these new developments but that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then there's a reference about five lines down where Karadzic says, "You see, Milad has wrong ideas but we've dealt with it." Do you recall who he is referring to when he refers to the name Milad and what the ideas are that he's referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't recall the conversation or this name Milad. It doesn't really sound like a name at all. It might have been Milosevic being just a first few sounds of his name but as I say that I was afraid, he might have been referring to Mr. Milosevic because I was really afraid that he might react more furiously to the adoption of this declaration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving over the page, you state to -- Karadzic tells you not to worry and then you say, "They have to give in now. He has found himself, particularly now after The Hague, he has found himself in a tight corner, I think," and then you tell Karadzic you are speaking about Alija. Do you recall why it was you thought Alija would have -- well, first of all, who is Alija, and secondly, do you recall why it was that thought he would have to give in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: It refers to Mr. Izetbegovic. The euphoria that prevailed up until the adoption of the declaration on the independence of the BiH subsided because now that they adopted it, what next? The Serbs were getting their ranks together, also in political terms, so what was going to be their next step, especially because we still had to deal with the preparations for the plebescite of the Serbian people to take place in November and of course it was certain that our people were going to vote in favour of remaining in Yugoslavia, but there might be other citizens of other ethnicities voting for voting for staying within Yugoslavia, so there was a possibility for that memorandum, for this declaration to actually fall through as a result of such a vote. These two parties that were forming this unprincipled political coalition at the time were working on the ground organising at the grass roots because Mr. Karadzic is mentioning Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now just before he mentions Travnik, he says, "So Croats are very busy with the regionalisation. They've made maps and rounded up the regions before we did." What was the situation in Bosnia as regards regionalisation as at October 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall these matters specifically because these were initiatives I did not take part in. I believe that the Serbian Democratic Party had a document containing Serb proposals. It was also a compromise-seeking document saying, Well this is the platform that we could try to reach an agreement over. I was more preoccupied with the plebescite at the time because my desire was to involve as many political parties in this initiative as possible and I wanted to ensure that all the citizens turned out to vote in favour of staying within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next point is where Travnik is mentioned. Karadzic says, "There will be a conflict because they want to take more," and he gives Travnik as an example. He says, "The Muslims make up a relative majority there and Croats want Travnik for themselves." What was your understanding in terms of the demographic, that is, the relative majority or minority, and the potential for conflict?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, this statement by Mr. Karadzic reflects the truth, that traditionally, Croats deem Travnik to be their own while, in actual fact, the Muslims had a majority there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you accept Mr. Karadzic's statement here there could be a conflict in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't focused on that part of our conversation because usually when I spoke to Mr. Karadzic, I had some sort of a plan where I wanted to get him involved. I tried to ensure through this conversation that we launch another initiative that would seek a compromise with the Muslims, because my point of view was somewhat different because we had different states coming into existence and then disappearing: The Ottoman Empire, the Austro-Hungarian Empire, then the state of the Slovenes, Croats and Serbs. The only permanent eternal thing there was the people, so the people are there and we should seek a certain solution. However, the atmosphere within the SDS was apparently such that Karadzic did not dare to even get involved into some sort of a discussion of that sort, such a political adventure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's clear from the conversation. Here you suggest a course of action, in terms of going public, and Karadzic firmly rejects that proposal. Just prior to him rejecting that proposal, he says to you -- he talks about historical rights and then he says, "And our territories are quite ethnically clean and we'll easily agree with the Muslims." Did you engage in discussions with Mr. Karadzic about those topics, about whether or not particular territories were ethnically clean and the effect that might have on agreements with Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: All these ethnic parties that formed government in Bosnia and Herzegovina that I myself had supported in a certain way in coming to power in order for the communism to become part of history, they had all lost themselves in history in these myths. I wasn't really following what was going on because I wasn't specifically interested in these stories. Because the Muslims wanted to have Bosnia-Herzegovina. They became great patriots. Now -- whereas -- as the Serbs, genetically we perceived Bosnia-Herzegovina as our own homeland, so how could they claim it to be their own if we, ourselves, feel that it is ours. The extremist Croat politics always envisaged to have Croatia up until the Drina River, so all of these peoples loved Bosnia-Herzegovina, yearned for it, and were on the lookout for a historical document that would substantiate their claim that Bosnia-Herzegovina was only their own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in answering my inquiries about this conversation, you mentioned that when you were speaking to Karadzic you had in mind certain programmes or plans that you wanted to discuss with him and these issues of regionalisation and whether or not territories were ethnically clean were other issues. Am I correct to say that these are not the issues that you focused on in your discussions with Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, these were not the issues. I wanted his support for the initiative that I was organising, namely the plebescite, where -- to which we wanted to invite members of all the different ethnicities and our preparation for the convention in Belgrade, because he had been in this group of parties for half a year already in favour of remaining within Yugoslavia. And that's what I had in mind -- that was the plan that I had in mind when I was talking to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to reiterate. We referred to the issue of regionalisation and as far as you were concerned, was that a matter for the SDS party and something you didn't involve yourself in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: On this issue, I wrote an article for Oslobodjenje where I said that some of them would perceive regionalisation as their savior and others would perceive it as an occupation and that was all that I could have done to speak my mind on it. But let's face it; that's not really much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could refer back to Exhibit 543, and if that could be presented to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, I refer to the last three paragraphs of this document, and that's the last portion of the third-last paragraph and the last two paragraphs. Is this the article that you're referring to where you referred to the setting up of autonomous regions? And in the second-last paragraph, you say: "If the ruling parties fail to bring their stance closer with regard to setting up autonomous regions and constituting a chamber of peoples, I fear, given there is no consensus in sight when between the SDA, SDS and HDZ on the fundamental issue, Yugoslavia as a federal state, yes or no, that the autonomous regions would be a life-saving solution for one nation, while for the other or others this would mean occupation or reason for armed rebellion." Then you proceed and say: "If this happens and if a war breaks out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, historic responsibility will be borne by all those who unscrupulously participate in the breakup of Yugoslavia with its millions of victims built into the state foundations." Is that -- does that accurately set out your views on the autonomous regions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly. Perhaps I could say something more on this issue. The Chamber of Peoples is mentioned here. An opportunity for the Chamber of Peoples to be introduced in the Assembly, which would make decisions by consensus, was -- was something that the earlier government had because they knew that they would lose -- they would be defeated in the multiparty elections because it was already clear from the Croatian and Slovenian examples that they would be defeated at the elections. So basically the new government after the elections inherited this chaotic situation and instead of putting it to order, just additionally made it more chaotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to refer to the next two exhibits, which are sessions of the Assembly of the Serbian People. The first one has previously been presented as P64 and P65, and that's the 24 October 1991 session. And the second one is the one which is 19 on the list, which is the 21st December 1991 session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that does not appear anywhere else in the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to be honest, that surprises me that my records suggest it hasn't, and I'm assured that it hasn't previously been presented in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, the shorthand record of the 4th Session of the Assembly of the Serbian People in BiH held on the 21st of December 1991 ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Prosecution Exhibit P545.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just inquire: These stenographic notes, are they -- they're different from the minutes, I take it? I remember that we had a discussion earlier on what version would best reflect the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm informed that on some occasions we have both the stenographic notes and the minutes, and that when we -- that we may have presented previously the stenographic notes -- we may have presented previously the minutes and now we're presenting the stenographic notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, did you attend the first session of the Assembly of the Serbian People on the 24th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did attend the Assembly session referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, can I refer you to page 51 of the minutes that are before you and do you see set up there a transcript of the speech that you delivered at this session?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, pages 51, 52 and 53, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I'm referring to page -- I'm not entirely clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And page 27 of the English, that's page 51 and continuing of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, is that an accurate record of a speech that you delivered at that session?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I will have to read it first to give you a definite answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Shall I read it out aloud?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, just if you read it to yourself to refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is indeed my speech delivered at that Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, in light of the discussions we've just had about your activities regarding the plebescite, I refer you to the concluding three paragraphs of your speech wherein you say the following and that is: "The latest session of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly has shown clearly that in this republic too there are efforts to outvote the Serbian people and push them into the margins, turn them into a national minority. "The representatives of the Serbian people in this republic have found an appropriate response: In a democratic manner, by a plebescite, they will say that they want to save this republic, that they want to save their shared state of Yugoslavia, and the Serbian Assembly should secure the national sovereignty of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina forever." And you say, "Let us hope that the Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina will not be forced to defend their legitimate rights with weapons like the Serbs in Croatia." Does that accurately portray your efforts as at 24 October 1991 to find a solution to the problems in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but there is one correction, however. I state correctly here the representatives of the Serbian people in this republic have found an adequate reply by democratic way. By plebescite they will say that they want to preserve also this republic which is Bosnia and Herzegovina and their joint state, their shared state of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter was translating not reading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what we mean is to preserve both Bosnia and Herzegovina and our joint state of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could move on to the next document that's being presented, and that is the minutes of the Assembly of 21 December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one question in between, Mr. Margetts. The last line where you say "Let us hope that the Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina will not be forced to defend the legitimate rights with weapons." How do I have to understand that? Is it to say that if others would not respect the right of the Serbs, that is, to make their own entity or to be in a federal structure with Serbia Montenegro that if this would not have been decided in favour of those rights, that the use of weapons would be the way to secure those rights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was drawing a parallel between circumstances in Bosnia and Herzegovina and those in Croatia. When the Serbs who, throughout the period after the Second World War had been a constituent nation in the Republic of Croatia, and according to all the Croatian constitutions, Croatia was a federal unit within the SFRY and it was a republic of the Serbian -- of the Croatian people and the Serbs in Croatia. But when the Serbs were chucked out of the constitution in Croatia, what happened there happened. I cannot say what exactly transpired because I wasn't living there. Now, I'm drawing -- this parallel situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina was similar. There was an unprincipled parliamentary majority formed that adopted a key document for the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina against the will of the Serbian deputies in the Bosnian parliament. So what I'm doing in this paragraph is drawing this parallel. Will the Serbs have to react in the same fashion as they had reacted in Croatia. This is just an analysis of the situation and a warning upon that analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand you make the comparison with Croatia where at least the position of the Serbs and the constitution had -- had changed. Was there any -- at that moment was there any indication apart from that Bosnia, at least, there was a wish among Muslims and Croats to make Bosnia and Herzegovina and independent state, but was there any proposal at that time to make the Serbs not any longer a constituent people or constituent nation of that independent republic, if it would come to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Interpretation after the adoption of the memorandum on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina there were no initiatives within the parliament to that effect, nor did I have any indication the effect that the war was on the horizon. But everything that was happening before that and what was happening at that particular moment actually induced me to think that war indeed was in store and I thought that the Serbs have been brought into a situation where they would, indeed, rise up in arms as they had in Croatia. It wasn't that it was just a political consideration that actually occurred to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time you say that, Let's hope that the Serbs will not be forced, immediately after you've told what should happen, that is, a plebescite, that they want to stay in Yugoslavia and that the Serbian Assembly should secure the national sovereignty of the Serb people so it sounds as if in the next line where you say "If this is not achieved, then the only way to defend these rights is to use arms."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, actually, if you observe this discussion in an isolated way, you can interpret it. But this was a few days after this unfortunate memorandum on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was adopted, so I gave the public release and I said there was the -- we had an instance of terror of this Assembly majority against Assembly minority and I was afraid that this could be translated in the field into terror of two peoples against a third people and that is how it could be seen. And another thing, it was quite sure that if, indeed, the Bosnia and Herzegovina was declared an independent state and internationally recognised, the situation in the field was such that it took only a little spark for a really wide-ranging conflagration because rage had sent in. On the one hand there was euphoria and on the other hand, there was rage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although it's not really an answer to my question, it gives at least some context. Let's move on, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, if I can refer you to the other document that we provided to you, which is the minutes of the session of the Assembly of the Serbian People of 21 December 1991, were you in attendance at that session?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that I attended all these Assembly sessions until the proclamation of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so probably I also attended this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I refer you to page 61 of this session and I invite you to read the speech that is accredited to you from page 61 through to page 65 and in the English, that is at page 30 through to page 31.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my speech at that Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, Dr. Djokanovic, could I refer you to the closing three paragraphs of this speech as well, and in these closing paragraphs you refer to Mr. Izetbegovic and you say that you "knew very well that the fate of Bosnia-Herzegovina fortunately or unfortunately, whether somebody likes it or not, is intrinsically linked to the fate of Yugoslavia. Yet he, for reasons that are only known to him, attacked Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina yesterday. This is what the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina have to realise unless they are biased, unless they want to dominate the Serbian people, by this I mean citizens who are not Serbs. The only objection that can be put to the Serbian people is that they are defending themselves. Only if the Serbian people have not got the right to self defence then they are wrong. In that case, this Assembly of the Serbian People should not have been established nor should the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina have been established. If the Serbian people have not got the right to defend themselves, the decision that have been made" - probably should read "has been made today" - and it says "are not legitimate." Maybe the decisions that have been made today are not legitimate. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What about looking at the original rather than to the English translation, Mr. Margetts. Do we have a -- apparently for reasons of shortage of originals, I haven't got the original but perhaps it could be put on the ELMO so the interpreters could see where the mistake it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's in plural, "decisions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That has been done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, does that accurately set out your idea as to the right of the Serbian people to defend themselves?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: This entire presentation is in this context. I'm talking about the political struggle, needless to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you provide a brief comment to the Court as to how the Assembly of the Serbian People was intended to defend the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: At this moment, we can only talk about what actually happened and that is that the Serbian Assembly was proclaimed after which we organised the plebescite of the Serbian people. Throughout 1990, I actually called for a referendum of the citizens to state their views on the future of Yugoslavia. First, there should have been a referendum within Bosnia and Herzegovina to see whether all the people were in favour of Yugoslavia. This was in early 1991. But the Serbian deputies had no other option, having been elected by the people and having been elected in the second half of 1990 when the political situation in Croatia had already become quite critical, had entered a quite critical stage and already smacked of war. So here, we had people electing their deputies not just like at any regular elections but in some sort of historic elections in order for the deputies to protect their interests. Now, we had the representatives of two peoples in contravention of the constitution and the laws and the rules of procedure of the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina adopting such a document as their basis which was contrary to all these pieces of legislation. So it was only normal for the deputies to organise themselves to protect the interests of the Serbian people. So they first established the Serbian people's Assembly which, having been fortunate enough, could have grown into a chamber of peoples during that period. So this intent of the Serbs to form a Serbian Assembly should have been interpreted by them as the Serbs wish to protect their interests and they should have said let's translate it into a chamber of peoples and then let us take all our future decisions by consensus but this is not the way it happened. This did not sit well with the Muslim side. At the time it was best not to be a Serb at all and not to have any political opinions and they said, We will declare Bosnia and Herzegovina independent and we shall then take proper care of you. And Alija Izetbegovic, in effect, said things which were patronising. He could not have said things to the Serbs, he could not have told the Serbs he would be protecting their interests in that way that he would be the protector of their interests in the future just as it would be illusory for Mr. Karadzic to have said at that particular point in time that he would be taking care and looking after the Muslims' interests because that was an unrealistic policy. So everything that was done was in my view the establishment of a good starting point, a position for the Serb people and the Serbian politicians for future negotiations, especially if we know that the conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina took place shortly thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I remind you of your speed of speech. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at the time you delivered that speech, which was December 1991, am I understanding your answer correctly to be that you saw the possibility for the Assembly of the Serbian People to, in some manner, unite with the continuing Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina rather than to establish an independent authority in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: To politically proclaim the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, if you do that, then of course you're not thinking of the other solution because I told you that the Serbs had perceived Bosnia-Herzegovina as their own state. They have so for a very long time. But then suddenly you are faced with this wave of patriotism on the side of the Muslims, even today, the Serbs are peaceful and calm and do not speak against Bosnia and Herzegovina, they do perceive it as their own but they do not wish to raise the issue of equality or of a nation every ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could move to the next exhibit, and I am actually going out of order here. That's now moving to Exhibit 25 which is the Assembly session of 18 March, 1992. And it's P64 and P65.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Margetts, since we promised Ms. Loukas to give her five minutes, could you find a suitable moment to stop in approximately seven minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I actually timed this particular topic and hadn't been mindful of the time that was assigned to Ms. Loukas, so if -- I can proceed but I'll need to proceed differently if I don't have until a quarter to which I'm quite happy to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's say use your next seven minutes in the way you find best.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, Your Honour, if we could move then to the series of intercepts which are the next in order, on the exhibit list. I don't see the necessity to play these intercepts into court, I'll just refer the witness to the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The CD of the intercept dated 26/12/1991 will be P546. The transcript will be P546A. The CD dated 29/12/1991 will be P547 and the transcript P547A. The CD dated 29 December 1991 between Radovan Karadzic and Dragan Djokanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem is that both of the 29th of December are the same interlocutors.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Bearing ERN number 0324-443424437 will be P548 and the transcript P548A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, you have before you transcripts of intercepts that purport to be intercepts of conversations between yourself and Radovan Karadzic. If you could cast your eye over those transcripts and inform the Court as to whether or not you recall having these discussions with Radovan Karadzic and if you don't recall the precise conversations, whether or not you recall having conversations of this nature with Radovan Karadzic during the end of -- toward the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: This is specifically 26th of December, it is the end of the year, but it's the 26th of December and that's important because that was the date when we, from Bosnia and Herzegovina, were in the federal Presidency, we discussed the confirmation and upon our -- the conference and upon our return to Sarajevo, we were discussing the way this meeting with the Presidency was covered and what the Muslim representatives who were at that meeting in Belgrade called -- were called. They were called political apparitions in such terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can I first of all refer you to this conversation of 26 December 1991 and to the final page where you organise with Dr. Karadzic when you'll meet him the next time and you say -- he says to you: "We should start offensively. Call Momo and start offensively from the Assembly." And you said, "All right. I've spoken to Momo so I thought we would get together tomorrow with regard to this convention." Who is the Momo who is being referred to by you and Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: We're referring to Mr. Krajisnik, the president of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, in terms of the organisation of the convention on Yugoslavia and the other matters that you're discussing in this intercept, did you have conversations with both Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: At this point, we returned to Sarajevo from the meeting with the Presidency of the SFRY. Thanks to the president, Mr. Krajisnik, we were given premises within the Assembly building to work on the proposal of -- for the draft convention of Yugoslavia and what Mr. Karadzic and I are talking about is the preparation of this meeting that we should meet in the premises of the Assembly building to work on the text. He thought it good to discuss these matters within the Assembly meeting -- the building, that it should be the Assembly building from where such initiatives are given support.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm mindful of the time and I'll continue these questions tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Djokanovic, we'll stop for the day. I'd like to instruct you not to speak to anyone about your testimony that you've given until now, that you're still about to give in the coming days. We'd like to see you back at 9.00 tomorrow morning in this same courtroom. Madam Usher, could you escort Mr. Djokanovic out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Just in relation to those housekeeping matters I referred to earlier today. Firstly in relation to the issue of P231, that revised translation has been received and reviewed and we have no objection to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So P231 is in its revised edition now and admitted into evidence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Secondly in relation to the issue of Mr. Bjelobrk, Your Honour has granted two weeks starting from the 7th of March and that's an issue that Mr. Stewart will deal with upon his return. Also thirdly, so that we don't have to go into private session to deal with that matter, that matter that involves private sessions is another matter that Mr. Stewart will deal with upon his return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: In relation to the Exhibits D34 and D35, our case manager has sent an e-mail to the Prosecution's case manager as there is some outstanding issues in relation to the audios there. The last matter, Your Honour, is the issue of the translation of P292.1/KID 31469. The Defence still has outstanding translation issues in relation to that particular exhibit and I will be forwarding those further -- a copy of -- a marked-up copy of those particular translation issues. For example, one of the issues was actually corrected on the transcript but it was not corrected in the translation so that, unfortunately, that particular exhibit we cannot put to rest at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the parties will continue to communicate with it and if there's any remaining issue, the Chamber will have to decide on -- we'll hear and then do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There is one matter I should alert the Trial Chamber to, and that is the fact that we're having enormous problems to find an interpreter for my conference with Mr. Krajisnik this afternoon at 6.00 but hopefully we can sort that out, but just to alert the Trial Chamber to the continuing problems of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that to the extent the registry is in a position to assist, that it will and if you, for whatever reasons, need to recruit an interpreter from somewhere else, then I hope you will be successful.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. The registry always tries to be very helpful in this regard and hopefully in some way we'll able to sort out this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there anything else you'd like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Nothing on behalf of the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I've got a question for you, Mr. Margetts. This witness was scheduled for eight hours. I notice that we are now at approximately the 26th of December, 1991. We heard a lot about alternative courses politicians might have taken and what alternatives there were that would have avoided a war to break out. Until now, apart from the appointment, we have hardly heard anything about his role as -- of this witness as a commissioner, the functioning of the Presidency when he was nearby, how people were appointed, how people would report. Well, from the impression we get, from the statement of the witness, there is still a lot to be done. We are halfway and we are not yet at the beginning of the armed conflict itself. Do you think you can manage to finish within the eight hours set?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, prior to your summation of where we stand, I was confident that we would. In terms of volume of material, we're exactly at the halfway point in terms of exhibits and my notes of this examination, and I've taken that that was a good indicator so I would expect that we'd be finished by the end of the third session tomorrow. There is a possibility that we may require the first session on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's good to hear that you're confident that you can still finish within the time limit you had set for yourself. At the same time, I take it that you also heard some of the in-between-the-lines observations on the relevance of what courses could have been taken which would have avoided war and of course it's never bad to establish that another cause would have been possible and that a war would not have broken, but sometimes it goes very much in detail and this is just one of the issues where you might get the impression that the political context is at the core of the case as to what happened at the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for those observations and we'll bear that in mind in the continuing examination of this witness and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of March, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
